children: Wheat for December delivery fell 1.9% to $7.13 1/2 a bushel on the Chicago Board of Trade Friday, with traders cutting long positions in wheat ahead of the weekend.
Soybeans for November fell 1.3% to $13.03 a bushel.
Corn for December delivery fell 0.6% to $5.27 1/4 a bushel.

Trimming the Top: Wheat futures led the way down for the grains complex on Friday. Traders pared risk ahead of U.S.-China negotiations starting next week, with wheat getting trimmed the most of long positions among grain futures. "To us, it appears as if funds have been selling Chicago wheat against their longs in the beans and the corn," Marex's Charlie Sernatinger said in a note. Traders next moves will on Monday following Friday's release of the CFTC's Commitment of Traders numbers.

Prepping for Volatility: Meetings between U.S. and Chinese officials took center stage for traders, particularly next week's talks between President Trump and Chinese President Xi. With Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent meeting his Chinese counterpart He Lifeng this weekend, the market sees a possibility of choppy trading when markets open next week. "Expect volatility to ramp up significantly next week with the China/U.S. talks," the Hightower Report in said a note, adding that "headline risk [is] extremely high."

Lowest Since 2010: Wheat exports out of Russia and Ukraine for the first quarter of the region's 2026/27 marketing year, which began in July, fell to the lowest level since 2010/11, according to SovEcon. Combined exports totaled 8 million metric tons for the quarter, compared to 16.2 mmt a year ago and a five-year average of 18.2 mmt. "The global market is therefore set to receive around 8.2 mmt less wheat than last year and about 10.2 mmt less than the recent average--equivalent to nearly half and almost 60%, respectively, of a typical month of global wheat trade," SovEcon said in a note.

Turning a Profit: U.S. harvesting is underway, but analysts are looking toward what 2027 crop budgets may look like. Input costs remain a tough obstacle for farmers to overcome, but Purdue University's new projections show that farm acres are expected to be profitable next year. The university's Center for Commercial Agriculture said that corn or soybean acres planted in Indiana next year could make farmers anywhere from just above $100 an acre to as much as nearly $470 an acre--depending on the quality of the soil and the rotation of their crops. "For average productivity soils, current contribution margin estimates range from about $200 to $350 per acre depending on the crop," Purdue said in a release accompanying the forecasts.

Actions and Words: Ahead of next week's meetings with China, the USDA announced a new flash sale of U.S. soybeans to the world's biggest agricultural buyer. The USDA said that 111,000 metric tons of soybeans have been sold to China for delivery in the 2026/27 marketing year. It's the first flash sale to China since Sept. 10. Next week's meetings are expected to have a lot of importance for U.S. agricultural trade. "China's recent U.S. soybean buying has increased the agricultural importance of the meeting," said Joe Davis of Futures International in a note.
The USDA will release its weekly Grain Export Inspections report at 11 a.m. ET Monday.
The USDA will release its weekly Crop Progress report at 4 p.m. ET Monday.
General Mills Inc. will release its first quarter 2027 earnings report at 7 a.m. ET Wednesday.
The EIA will release its Weekly Petroleum Status Update report at 10:30 a.m. ET Wednesday.
